The history of buttock and thigh claudication that takes some time to achieve
resolution is typical of lumbar spinal stenosis. One feature which helps
differentiate it from other causes of lower limb nerve pain is the normal straight
leg raise. MRI is the diagnostic modality of choice; typical features include loss of
epidural fat on T1-weighted images, loss of cerebrospinal fluid signal around the
dural sac on T2-weighted images, and degenerative disc disease. Decompressive
lumbar laminectomy is the usual first line surgical intervention.

and claudication related to vascular disease resolves more quickly.

A 67-year-old woman presents to the General Medical Clinic with long-standing                   Difficulty: Easy
pain in her hands. She has had progressively worsening deformity of her hands
with ongoing pain and stiffness. She has no systemic symptoms. For many years,
she has been taking only paracetamol and ibuprofen as this has controlled her
pain, but she finds this to be no longer effective. She has a past medical history
of asthma as a child, elective hip replacement due to osteoarthritis and
On examination of her hands there is painful swelling of wrists and
Blood tests have been requested.                                                         Expanded
W hat is the most appropriate management plan?
This patient has chronic deformity due to underlying, untreated rheumatoid
arthritis (RA). There is also evidence of active synovitis. The deformity in this
patient includes ulnar deviation of the metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joints, radial
shift of metacarpals, Boutonniere deformity of the thumb and swan-neck
While the aim of treatment is to prevent this level of deformity, the joint pain also
indicates active disease. This means that treatment is needed with a disease-
modifying antirheumatic drug (DMARD) to help control disease in the long term
and a corticosteroid to achieve disease control in the short term.
Biological therapy includes adalimumab and etanercept. These are monoclonal
antibodies which can be used as treatment when DMARD therapy has failed in
RA. It is not appropriate as first-line therapy.
Codeine is a mild opiate which can be used as analgesia. It would not help in
addressing the underlying problem for this patient.
Methotrexate can be used as first-line treatment to control RA, but the active
synovitis means that corticosteroids are necessary to induce remission as well.
Topical non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) creams are useful in hand
and knee osteoarthritis, but would not be useful in addressing the underlying RA
in this patient and would fail to prevent further deformity.

This patient has polymyalgia rheumatica (PMR). PMR is an

characterised by proximal muscle pain and stiffness, which is worse in
the morning and improves throughout the day. It should not be
confused with polymyositis or diseases that cause proximal myopathy,

stiffness of the shoulder and hip girdles. Distal joint stiffness is not
seen and is usually a sign of a different inflammatory arthritis such as
rheumatoid arthritis (RA). MCP joint stiffness is a common presenting

Proximal muscle weakness is not a symptom of PMR. Rather, proximal

lymphocytic leukaemia is brought to the Emergency Department by
her partner. For the past few weeks she has been suffering increasing            Peer Responses %
proximal myopathy and bony pain, predominantly affecting the long
bones of the arms and legs. Blood testing reveals profoundly low
phosphate levels. Urine testing reveals the presence of glycosuria,
W hat diagnosis fits best with this clinical picture?
Certain tumours, including mesenchymal tumours, adenocarcinomas
(e.g. prostatic carcinoma) and haematological malignancies such as         Clinical Presentation
myeloma and chronic lymphocytic leukaemia, appear to produce a
phosphaturic substance. They secrete fibroblast growth factor 23           Differential Diagnosis
(FGF23) and other phosphaturic proteins. Most affected patients have
increased circulating FGF23 levels. The primary transport protein          Diagnosis / Investigation
responsible for phosphate reabsorption in the kidney is the type II
sodium-phosphate co-transporters (NaPi-IIa and NaPi-IIc) localised in      Management
FGF23 decreases reabsorption of phosphate and production of 1,25-
dihydroxy vitamin D by the kidney, acting via FGF receptor 1 (FGFR1)
signaling. The resulting hypophosphatemia causes rickets,
osteomalacia, bone pain, muscle weakness, and fractures, usually
accompanied by a marked reduction in concentration of 1,25-OH
vitamin D. Other abnormalities of renal function such as glycosuria and
aminoaciduria may also be present occasionally . Treatment with
vitamin D metabolites and phosphate supplements may result in some
resolution of skeletal symptoms. In the case of solid tumours, removal
of the primary tumour also results in improvement of symptoms.
Hypoparathyroidism is associated with hypocalcaemia and increased
phosphate, and is unlikely here given there has been no surgery that
could have led to secondary hypoparathyroidism.
X-linked hypophosphataemia presents with symptoms of rickets in
childhood. It is X-linked dominant, with more severe symptoms in boys
and is treated with calcitriol and phosphate supplementation.
Tumour lysis syndrome is associated with induction chemotherapy, and
is primarily manifest by hyperkalaemia and decreased renal function.
Primary hyperparathyroidism is associated with hypercalcaemia and
secondary hyperparathyroidism with renal impairment, neither of
which are reported here on blood testing.

C     Avascular necrosis of the hips
Deprivation of blood supply to the cortex and medulla results in
marrow cell death and causes AVN. The common causes are lupus,
high-dose corticosteroid therapy, antiphospholipid antibody syndrome,
sickle cell disease, alcoholism, Caisson’s disease and Gaucher’s
disease. In lupus, femoral head involvement is the most common and
in 90% of cases progresses to involve the opposite side after 12
months. The pain is often most severe and recalcitrant, with poor
response to analgesic and anti-inflammatory medications. CRP and
ESR may show mild/moderate elevation in this condition, or may be
normal. Indeed no particular blood parameter is useful for diagnosis or
assessing prognosis of this condition. Plain X-ray characteristically
shows irregular contouring of the femoral head, although it may
appear normal in the early phase. MRI is the most sensitive modality of
imaging for AVN of the hip, and is the investigation of choice in
patients where AVN is suspected but radiography is normal.
Conservative treatment involves non-weight bearing to prevent the
collapse of the femoral head and secondary osteoarthritis. Depending
on the stage of the disease, surgical options include core
decompression or replacement of the femoral head.
